newsitem.title: USA: Critics vow to fight Colorado water project.
newsitem.headline: Critics vow to fight Colorado water project.

text.p: Congressional opponents of a major water project in southern Colorado vowed Thursday to block more funding for the long-delayed plan to supply water to local communities, industry, and Native Americans.

A Senate subcommittee earlier this week recommended providing $6 million in the 1998 fiscal year to back negotiations to revise the Animas-La Plata project, although $8 million remains unspent from this year.
"Eight million can fund a heck of a lot of talk," Rep. Peter DeFazio, an Oregon Democrat, said at a news conference. "No further appropriations should be made."

The project to divert water from the Animas River to the La Plata River was expected to cost the federal government about $500 million of a total project cost of $740 million. But supporters this week proposed scaling back the plan to $290 million, with the U.S. government to bear $260 million.

Wisconsin's Democratic Sen. Russ Feingold and Republican Rep. Tom Petri, who led opposition to the original Animas-La Plata project, said Congress should not approve any new funding until a new plan has been endorsed by lawmakers.

"I do not support the search for alternatives if the taxpayers continue to be asked to sock money away in the Bureau of Reclamation's construction account as a placeholder for an option that has not yet been fully analyzed," Feingold said in a statement.

Critics have tried to kill the project, which grew out of a water rights settlement with Native Americans, because they said it had a huge price tag, caused environmental harm, and gave only one-third of the diverted water to the tribes.
Under the new proposal, the tribes would get a bigger share of the water supply, but the total volume they would receive is one-third less than under the original plan.

The Southern Ute Grassroots Organization said instead of supporting the water project, it wanted the federal government to set up a $100 million fund to help the tribes buy land and water rights on the open market wherever they wanted in their area.
Attorneys for the Sierra Club and other opponents of Animas-La Plata said they planned to present a land and water rights fund proposal to negotiators by the end of this month.
